bacb7ee18094eeca: Amasra is a small Black Sea coastal town known in ancient times as Amastris; it is believed to have taken its name from a Persian princess who ruled the region. It is situated on a peninsula featuring the remains of walls and a castle dating back to the Byzantine and Genoese periods. The town’s two natural coves, known as the Big Harbor and the Small Harbor, give it its distinctive appearance. With its small scale, fishing village atmosphere, and historic character, it is one of the well-known day-trip destinations along the Black Sea coast.
34a9b0b29eecf2d0: Istanbul is known for being the only major city that spans two continents—one in Europe and one in Asia. It served as the capital of the Byzantine Empire (as Constantinople) and, later, the Ottoman Empire for centuries. Hagia Sophia—first a Byzantine cathedral, then a mosque, a museum for many years, and now a mosque once again—and the Sultanahmet (Blue) Mosque are among the city’s iconic landmarks. The Grand Bazaar is considered one of the world’s oldest and largest covered markets. Topkapı Palace served as the administrative and residential center for the Ottoman sultans for approximately 400 years. The Bosphorus is the strait that physically divides the city between two continents.
9ba0afef18abb95a: Cappadocia is famous for its intriguing rock formations known as “fairy chimneys,” which were formed by thousands of years of erosion of volcanic tuff. The region has become one of the world’s most renowned destinations for hot-air balloon tours. Underground cities such as Derinkuyu and Kaymaklı—carved into the rock by early Christians as shelters and places of worship—along with rock-cut churches featuring Byzantine-era frescoes on their walls, showcase the region’s rich history. Göreme National Park and the Rock Sites of Cappadocia were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985.
95a41a90bdf61c7d: Antalya is one of Turkey’s best-known tourist destinations on the Mediterranean coast and is located in the ancient region of Pamphylia. The Hadrian Gate, dating from the Roman period, and the Düden Waterfall in the city center are among its main landmarks. The ancient cities in the surrounding area—Aspendos, with its Roman theater that is still used for events today; Termessos, perched on a mountainside; and the port city of Perge—make the region significant in terms of the ancient world’s heritage. The city is known as one of the main gateways to modern beach tourism in Turkey.
554269b6e23c25d5: Bodrum was known as Halicarnassus in ancient times and was home to the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus (the monumental tomb of King Mausolus—the origin of the word “mausoleum”), which was considered one of the Seven Wonders of the World. Bodrum Castle (St. Peter’s Castle) was built by the Knights of Rhodes and today houses the Museum of Underwater Archaeology. With its whitewashed architecture and vibrant nightlife, it has become one of Turkey’s most famous Aegean resort towns.
947352bfded3aab7: Trabzon was one of the major port cities on the historic Silk Road along the Black Sea and served as the capital of the Empire of Trebizond, a successor state to the Byzantine Empire, from 1204 to 1461. One of the city’s most famous landmarks is the Sumela Monastery, a Greek Orthodox monastery built on the slope of a cliff. It is also known for its own Hagia Sophia (a structure from the Byzantine era, distinct from the one in Istanbul, which has undergone transformations from a mosque to a museum and back to a mosque). The region is also recognized as one of Turkey’s leading hazelnut-producing centers.
aa8dcd566e205e4b: Fethiye, known in ancient times as Telmessos, is a city renowned for its magnificent Lycian rock tombs carved into the cliffs (particularly the Amyntas Rock Tomb). Ölüdeniz (Blue Lagoon) Beach and paragliding from Babadağ above it are among the region’s most famous activities. The Lycian Way long-distance hiking trail begins here. Nearby Kayaköy is known as a Greek village that was abandoned following the 1923 population exchange.
c4f45ac5e2f28d33: Çeşme is an Aegean coastal town named after the historic fountains in the town and known for the Çeşme Castle, which dates back to the Genoese-Ottoman period. The region is known for the Çeşme watermelon, prized for its distinctive flavor, and for its coves ideal for windsurfing.
5a3240af7efefc97: Izmir, known as Smyrna in ancient times and cited in many ancient sources as the birthplace of Homer, is a historic Aegean port city. The Izmir Clock Tower in Konak Square is the city’s most recognizable landmark.
